When you say something figuratively, you are using language in an imaginative, non-literal way — not to describe exact reality, but to paint a picture, express an emotion, or make an idea more vivid and powerful.

The single most important thing to understand about "figuratively" is what it sits across from: literally.

Literally = exactly as the words say, in real life.
Figuratively = not exactly as the words say, but conveying a deeper truth through imagery or comparison.

When you speak figuratively, the words you use are not meant to be taken at face value. You are borrowing an image from one thing to describe another thing — because that borrowed image captures the feeling or meaning far better than plain words would.

"I'm so hungry, I could eat a horse."

No one believes you can actually consume an entire horse. You are speaking figuratively — you are borrowing the extreme, ridiculous image of eating a horse to express the intensity of your hunger. The statement is not literally true, but it is emotionally and expressively true. It communicates something real about how you feel, just not through a factual description.

If you wanted to be precise, you could say:

"I'm so hungry I could eat a horse — figuratively speaking, of course."

The phrase "figuratively speaking" is a common way people signal: "I know this isn't literally true; I'm using an image to express myself."

Human language is not a cold reporting machine. We don't just transfer facts — we share feelings, ideas, and experiences. Figurative language is one of the most natural tools for doing this.

Consider these two sentences describing the same thing:

"She was very angry." — plain and accurate, but flat.

"She was figuratively breathing fire." — not literally true (she is not a dragon), but it puts a vivid, powerful image in your head. You feel her anger.

Figurative language makes communication more alive, more memorable, and more emotionally resonant. This is why poets, novelists, speakers, and ordinary people use it constantly.
The Kinds of Language That Are "Figurative"

When we say something is said figuratively, it usually falls into one of these forms. You don't need to memorize the names — just understanding what they have in common is enough.

Metaphors — saying one thing is another thing, to reveal a similarity:

"Life is a journey."

Life is not literally a journey with a road and a destination, but describing it figuratively as one helps us understand that it has a path, direction, choices, and an end.

Hyperbole — deliberate, extreme exaggeration to emphasize:

"I've told you a million times."

Not literally a million. Figuratively, it means: many, many times — enough to feel exhausting.

Similes — comparing one thing to another using like or as:

"She runs like the wind."

She is not literally the wind. Figuratively, she runs with great, effortless speed.

Idioms — fixed expressions where the words together mean something different from their individual meanings:

"He kicked the bucket."

He did not literally kick a bucket. Figuratively (idiomatically), he died.

"She let the cat out of the bag."

No actual cat was involved. She accidentally revealed a secret.

All of these — when you use them — are examples of speaking figuratively.

The adverb "figuratively" is used to describe the manner of speaking or meaning. It tells you how something is meant — not literally, but through imagery.

"He figuratively carried the weight of the world on his shoulders."

He had enormous responsibilities and stress — not an actual globe sitting on him.

"The performance figuratively set the stage on fire."

It was electrifying and spectacular — the stage did not actually burn.

"She figuratively moved mountains to make the event happen."

She overcame huge obstacles and made extraordinary effort.

"The whole city figuratively held its breath waiting for the result."

Everyone was in a state of anxious suspense.

In each case, "figuratively" is there to tell you: interpret these words through the image they create, not through their literal meaning.
The Most Important Distinction: Figuratively vs. Literally

This is the distinction that matters most in everyday language, and also the one most often confused.

Forget the table — let's just be direct.

"Literally" means: this is exactly, factually, really happening.

"I literally fell asleep during the meeting." → You actually, physically fell asleep.

"Figuratively" means: this is not factually happening, but the image expresses the truth of it.

"I figuratively fell asleep during the meeting." → The meeting was so boring it felt like falling asleep — but you stayed awake.

A very common error in modern speech is using "literally" when the speaker actually means "figuratively":

"I literally died laughing."

You did not die. You are alive and speaking. The correct word here is figuratively — the feeling of laughing so hard felt, expressively, like dying.

This error is so widespread that dictionaries have noted it, but precision matters. If you want to be accurate: when the thing didn't actually happen but you're using the image to express intensity, the word is figuratively.
Recognizing When Something Is Meant Figuratively

A useful test: Could this sentence be true in reality?

"He has ice in his veins before a big game."

Ice in his veins? Literally impossible and fatal. So this is figurative — it means he is extremely calm under pressure.

"She has butterflies in her stomach."

No actual butterflies. Figurative — she is nervous.

"The news hit him like a ton of bricks."

No bricks involved. Figurative — the news shocked him intensely.

Whenever the literal meaning is impossible, absurd, or obviously not what was intended, the speaker is using language figuratively.

The phrase "figuratively speaking" is used as a gentle flag — a way of signaling in advance (or in retrospect) that you are about to use, or just used, figurative language.

"The project is, figuratively speaking, a runaway train."

You're warning the listener: I'm about to use an image — don't take it literally.

It is especially useful when the figurative expression might otherwise be misunderstood, or when you want to add a slight wink to your language — acknowledging that you're being expressive rather than factual.

Figuratively means: in a way that uses imaginative language — metaphors, exaggerations, comparisons, idioms — rather than literal, factual description.

When something is said figuratively, the words are not meant exactly as they stand. They borrow an image, a comparison, or an exaggeration to express a feeling, an idea, or a truth more vividly than plain language could.

It is the opposite of literally (which means exactly as stated, in reality).

The next time you hear "I'm going to kill him" from a frustrated friend, or "she has nerves of steel," or "time flies" — those are all figurative. The words are doing imaginative work, not factual reporting. And the adverb that describes that kind of language? Figuratively.
